abstract: Background: Social behaviour in mice is commonly assessed using standardized assays such as the three-chambered task, which provide controlled measures of sociability but often capture behaviour over short timeframes that may not capture the complex behavioural repertoire exhibited in the home environment. Although automated home-cage monitoring enables continuous, longitudinal assessment of group-housed mice with minimal human interference, methods for quantifying social behaviour in this complex setting remain limited. Information theory offers a framework for measuring statistical dependence between animals but requires one to account for dependence related to the cage environment that arise even in the absence of social interaction. Methods: We developed an information-theoretic approach to quantify social dependence using longitudinal RFID-based positional data from group-housed mice monitored with automated home-cage monitoring system. Mutual information (MI) between cagemates was evaluated against a constrained null model that disrupted within-cage dependence while preserving individual movement patterns. We used two strains with known differences in sociability (C57BL/6J and BTBR) to assess sensitivity to various temporal sampling parameters, test-retest reliability, and correspondence with manually video-scored social behaviours. We further examined variation across genetic backgrounds and investigated relationships between home-cage measures, conventional behavioural assays (three-chamber sociability and open-field behaviour), and brain structure using in vivo MRI. Results: Observed MI was distinguishable from our null distribution, validating its use to quantify statistical dependence beyond that expected from shared cage constraints. MI recapitulated known differences in sociability between C57BL/6J and BTBR mice, showed high test-retest reliability, and correlated with independently video-scored social behaviours. Home-cage social measures also varied across genetic backgrounds and captured strain differences separate from three-chamber sociability. Furthermore, in vivo MRI revealed distinct neuroanatomical patterns for home cage compared to three-chamber sociability measures, including brain regions implicated in social behaviour. Comparisons with open-field measures further indicated that home-cage information-theoretic measures capture behavioural variation not fully represented by conventional measures of locomotion and exploration. Finally, social coordination exhibited distinct temporal dynamics across the circadian cycle. Conclusion: This study establishes and validates an information-theoretic framework for quantifying social dependence from longitudinal home-cage positional data. By accounting for dependence arising from shared environmental constraints and demonstrating reproducibility and correspondence with observed social behaviour, this approach provides a complementary method for characterizing social behaviour in mice. Its application across genetic backgrounds and temporal contexts offers opportunities to investigate behavioural variation beyond the restricted sampling of conventional assays.
